paper_title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI systems built around large models increasingly use experience and feedback to make persistent changes to models, prompts, memories, tools, and workflows. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) extends this process to inductive biases and to the mechanisms that govern future updates, which can themselves be revised and reused across improvement cycles. Yet self-modification alone does not guarantee trustworthy improvement. Reported gains may reflect flawed evaluations, previously acquired capabilities may deteriorate, and compliance with behavioral constraints may weaken. Compromised artifacts or sensitive information may also persist in successor systems. Changes to improvement mechanisms may invalidate earlier verification results and make human oversight less effective. This survey presents an operational definition and process framework for RSI and organizes the requirements for trustworthy RSI into four interconnected themes: genuine and sustained improvement; behavioral constraints, alignment, and fairness; system security and privacy; and transparency and controllability. We examine these themes from three perspectives: Improvement Validity, Constraint Preservation, and Effective Oversight. This analysis covers improvement diagnosis, proposal generation, proposal evaluation, and update implementation (S1--S4), including the recursive application of these stages to improvement mechanisms (RI). We review risks, safeguards, and evaluation evidence for individual updates, effects inherited by successor systems, and revisions to improvement mechanisms, while distinguishing direct RSI findings from evidence in related systems. Finally, we examine evaluation settings, identify requirements for independent and longitudinal assessment, and discuss applications and open research problems.

Introduction [T]he system of nature, of which man is part, tends to be self-balancing, self-adjusting, self-cleansing. Not so with technology. . . E. F. Schumacher (1973) 1.1. Motivation Advances in LLMs, including GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026) and Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026), have improved broad range of capabilities, such as coding, tool use, and multi-step task execution. Building on these capabilities, self-evolving systems can use experience and feedback to introduce persistent changes to model parameters, memories, tools, and workflows, allowing these changes to influence subsequent tasks (Gao et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026e; Zweiger et al., 2025). Recursive self4 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges improvement (RSI) extends self-evolution by allowing systems to revise and reuse the mechanisms that govern subsequent updates. Recent research has explored this capability through editable meta-agents (Zhang et al., 2026g), evolving exploration strategies (Zheng et al., 2026c), and modular or regularized harness evolution (Wu et al., 2026d; Xia et al., 2026). These systems make the improvement procedure itself an explicit target of revision. Recursive updates can also preserve security vulnerabilities. Hyperagents allows meta-agent In to modify both task agent and its own improvement procedure (Zhang et al., 2026g). benchmark-poisoning experiment, tasks using self-signed certificates prompted the meta-agent to add persistent instruction directing the task agent to bypass HTTPS certificate verification. Successors inherited these instructions and generated insecure code on benign, held-out tasks, even after further evolution on clean benchmark (Roesner and Kohno, 2026). The experiment connects contaminated evaluation feedback to security failures in later successors. It motivates checking the validity of improvement evidence and the preservation of security requirements across revisions. When the improvement mechanism changes, the evaluations and safeguards governing later updates also require reassessment. These risks call for broad view of trustworthiness that considers reliability alongside safety, security, fairness, privacy, and transparency (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023). We organize the survey into four trustworthiness themes under three complementary analytical roles. The first theme, genuine and sustained improvement, addresses Improvement Validity by examining whether reported gains reflect genuine improvements in the intended capabilities and persist over time. Constraint Preservation is addressed through two themes: behavioral constraints, alignment, and fairness; and system security, resilience, privacy, and data governance. Together, these themes examine whether applicable requirements remain satisfied across successive updates. The fourth theme, transparency and controllability, addresses Effective Oversight by examining whether system changes remain understandable, auditable, and subject to authorized human intervention. We assess these requirements across individual updates, changes inherited by successor systems, and revisions to the improvement mechanism. Genuine and sustained improvement. This theme concerns whether reported gains reflect genuine improvements that persist across subsequent revisions. At the update level, acceptance scores can increase even as external correctness declines (Song et al., 2026). Across successors, accumulated skills may impair retrieval and task performance (Zhang et al., 2026k). When improvement mechanisms also revise evaluation criteria, higher scores may reflect changes in what is measured rather than actual performance gains. Behavioral constraints, alignment, and fairness. This theme concerns whether system behavior remains safe, aligned with relevant human goals and constraints, and fair to affected individuals or groups. Even benign fine-tuning or accumulated experience can weaken safety (Qi et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2026b), while adaptive exploration may produce biased allocations (Wu et al., 2026a). Such deviations may persist in successor systems, while changes to experience selection or reward mechanisms can further reinforce undesirable behavior. Revisions to behavioral requirements require authorization and evaluation of their effects on safety, alignment, and affected groups. System security, resilience, privacy, and data governance. This theme concerns protecting system components against malicious interference and ensuring the appropriate handling of sensitive information. Poisoned memories can redirect subsequent actions (Dong et al., 2025), while stored interactions may expose private information (Wang et al., 2025a). These risks may persist when compromised components or sensitive information are inherited by successors. If improvement mechanisms can also modify validation, access control, or data retention rules, the effectiveness of existing protections must be reassessed. 5 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges Transparency and controllability. This theme concerns whether system changes can be understood, traced, and corrected through effective human oversight. For individual updates, reviewers must be able to identify what changed and why it was accepted. As changes accumulate across successors, their effects must remain auditable and subject to correction or rollback. If improvement mechanisms can also modify auditing or rollback procedures, subsequent revisions may undermine the effectiveness of oversight itself. Accordingly, this survey addresses the following research questions. Key Questions RQ1 How can genuine improvements be demonstrated and shown to persist across successive revisions? RQ2 How can behavioral constraints, alignment, and fairness be preserved as systems and their improvement mechanisms evolve? RQ3 How can security, resilience, privacy, and authorized data use be maintained across inherited states and revisions to update mechanisms? RQ4 How can recursive updates remain transparent, auditable, and subject to [3] [4] [5] [6] effective human control? 1.2. Scope and Perspective We focus on RSI in large-model systems, where changes to models, prompts, memories, tools, and workflows can persist across successor versions. Beyond such persistent changes, RSI allows systems to revise and reuse the mechanisms guiding subsequent improvements. Human approval may remain part of this process. We analyze improvement diagnosis, proposal generation, proposal evaluation, and update implementation (S1S4), together with their recursive application to the improvement mechanism (RI). These categories locate risks, safeguards, and evidence requirements across different system architectures. Our review focuses on RSI research while drawing on related studies of persistent updates to inform specific risks, safeguards, and evaluation assumptions. We distinguish findings demonstrated directly in RSI from evidence obtained in related systems and prospective arguments. 1.3. Contributions Our main contributions are as follows: An operational definition and process framework for RSI. Building on the definition of machine learning proposed by Mitchell (Mitchell, 1997), we define RSI in terms of autonomous improvement of the inductive bias and recursive revision of its update function . We organize the improvement process into four stages: diagnosing limitations (S1), generating candidate revisions (S2), evaluating proposals (S3), and implementing accepted updates (S4). RI denotes the recursive application of these stages to itself. unified taxonomy and evidence-oriented synthesis. We organize four interconnected trustworthiness themes under three complementary analytical roles: Improvement Validity, Constraint Preservation, and Effective Oversight. Within this framework, we compare risks, safeguards, and evaluation methods across individual updates, successor systems, and revisions to improvement mechanisms, with versioned evidence map that distinguishes study-level coverage from joint evidence on aligned trajectories. We distinguish findings demonstrated directly in RSI from evidence obtained in related systems, as well as potential risks and proposed safeguards that have not yet been empirically validated. Longitudinal evaluation and open research problems. We specify paired continuations for assessing updater revisions, distinguish mechanism effects from total-cost efficiency, and identify open questions in capability retention, constraint preservation, evaluation independence, and effective intervention. 1.5. Section 7 reviews existing evaluation settings and develops evidence requirements for trustworthy RSI, covering longitudinal evaluation, causal assessment of recursive improvement, evaluator independence, and joint assessment of trustworthiness requirements. Finally, Section 8 synthesizes existing findings and their limitations, explores application settings at the intersection of RSI and trustworthiness, and discusses open problems and future research directions. Recursive Self-Improvement: Definition and Process The definition specifies what changes during RSI; the four-stage cycle describes how those changes are proposed, evaluated, and retained. 2.1.1. Definition of Recursive Self-Improvement We start from Mitchells definition of machine learning: Definition (Machine Learning) (Mitchell, 1997) computer program is said to learn from experience1E with respect to some class of tasks and performance measure P, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E. Generalizing beyond observed experience requires an inductive bias B: preferences that guide the choice among candidate policies consistent with the observed data (Mitchell, 1980). Formally, given experience E, we write learning system as follows: = A(B, E), (1) where denotes the learned policy, and denotes the inductive bias governing how learns. In conventional machine learning systems, the inductive bias is typically specified in advance 1Silver and Sutton (2025) emphasize that experience is generated through an agents interaction with its environment. Here, experience refers to broader concept that encompasses any data that can contribute to improving the systems learning performance. 9 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges and held fixed during learning. It may be embodied in the strategy for acquiring data, the formulation of the objective function, the choice of hypothesis space, the design of the optimization algorithm, or the criteria for evaluating learned models. In large-model systems, the learned policy in Eq. (1) may be realized by standalone model or by model together with prompts, memory, skills, and tools. The inductive bias specifies how that policy is learned or revised, including its initialization, training objectives, data selection rules, and optimization procedures. The distinction is functional: prompt that controls task execution belongs to h, whereas one that governs the construction or selection of policy updates belongs to B. For example, an instruction to run tests before submitting patch is part of h; rule for selecting corrected trajectories for training is part of B. The bias update function governs revisions to these learning choices and can itself be revised and reused in RSI. shared prompt or module may serve more than one role, so its effects on task execution and on each update process should be identified separately. These roles are defined relative to the task policy being evaluated and kept consistent across improvement cycles. We define RSI as follows. Definition (Recursive Self-Improvement, RSI) RSI is process in which learning system updates its policy from new experience, autonomously revises its inductive bias, and revises and reuses the mechanism for future bias updates, with the aim of sustained gains in task performance. Formally, let index completed improvement cycles, including cycles in which no revision is accepted. The states ht, Bt, and Ut are the components retained at the end of cycle t. RSI can be expressed as follows: ht+1 = ABt (ht, Et+1), (Bt+1, Ut+1) = Ut(Bt, ht+1, Ft+1), (2) (3) In Eq. (2), Et+1 is new experience and ABt is the learning process under the current inductive bias Bt. In Eq. (3), Ft+1 is feedback on performance and prior improvement attempts, and Ut is the bias update function. The resulting Bt+1 and Ut+1 are retained for subsequent cycles. These equations summarize complete improvement cycles. The operators include diagnosis, proposal generation, evaluation, and implementation, whose stages are shown as S1S4 in Figure 3. Their outputs denote the states retained after S4. Each component without an accepted revision retains its previous value. The policy update uses Bt; accepted changes to Bt and Ut govern later improvement cycles. Across improvement cycles, the bias update function Ut can revise the inductive bias Bt. The function Ut can itself be revised to Ut+1, which is used in the next cycle. Feedback Ft includes signals derived from data, environmental interaction, or self-evaluation. Conventional machine learning and reinforcement learning typically update task policies under specified learning rules (Mitchell, 1997; Sutton and Barto, 2018). In model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML), the learned initialization changes under prescribed meta-gradient procedure (Finn et al., 2017). Auto-sklearn selects algorithms and hyperparameters within specified search procedure (Feurer et al., 2015). Learned optimizers illustrate the distinction between an update rule and the procedure that trains it (Andrychowicz et al., 2016). When an optimizer governs updates to the task policy, it forms part of B, while its outer training procedure plays the role of . Training the optimizer changes B; revising and reusing that outer procedure also changes . Classification therefore depends on which component is revised and how it is subsequently used. Under the functional distinction above, task prompts contribute to h, mutation prompts specify part of B, and the prescribed hypermutation procedure plays the role of . This provides an example of evolving under fixed . Gödel machines provide theoretical account of self-revision in which system can rewrite its software, including its proof searcher, after proving the rewrite useful under its current utility function and axioms (Schmidhuber, 2006). The additional RSI condition in this survey is that the mechanism for revising is itself revised and reused in later cycles. The RSI Process in the Era of Large Models Eqs. (2) and (3) describe how the learned policy h, inductive bias B, and bias update function evolve across improvement cycles. The process view makes explicit how potential improvements are identified, proposed, evaluated, and incorporated into the system. Figure 3 illustrates these steps as four-stage improvement cycle (S1S4), together with its recursive application to the bias update function (RI). (S1) Improvement Diagnosis. The system uses the current policy ht, inductive bias Bt, experience Et+1, and feedback Ft+1 to identify limitations in its behavior or learning process. It determines whether addressing these limitations requires revisions to ht, Bt, or both, and defines the improvement objective that subsequent proposals should address. (S2) Proposal Generation. Based on the diagnosis from S1, the system generates candidate revisions to ht through the learning process ABt or to Bt through the bias update function Ut. These candidates may modify the learned policy or the choices and configurations that govern its learning. At this stage, the proposed revisions have not yet been incorporated into the system. (S3) Proposal Evaluation. The system evaluates candidate revisions against the current evaluation and acceptance criteria. It assesses whether the proposed changes address the identified limitations and satisfy the declared requirements, including checks for performance regressions on other tasks. The system then determines which revisions should be accepted based on the evaluation results. (S4) Update Implementation. The system incorporates accepted revisions into the successor system and retains the resulting ht+1 and Bt+1 for subsequent improvement cycles. Any component without an accepted revision remains unchanged. (RI) Recursive Improvement. The system applies S1S4 recursively to the bias update function Ut itself. If revision is accepted, the resulting Ut+1 is retained and reused in subsequent cycles, potentially changing how inductive biases are updated. Otherwise, Ut+1 = Ut. Three variants of coding agent illustrate these distinctions. In each variant, execution trajectories and corrected solutions provide Et+1, while test outcomes provide Ft+1. The task objective, externally specified acceptance criteria, and resource budget remain fixed. Trustworthiness: Concepts and Requirements Trustworthiness concerns whether reliance on an AI system is justified for its intended use (Li et al., 2023; National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023). Existing frameworks characterize trustworthiness in different ways. Li et al. (2023) distinguish technical and ethical requirements, while NIST identifies seven characteristics, including validity and reliability, security and resilience, and accountability and transparency (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023). TrustLLM identifies eight dimensions: truthfulness, safety, fairness, robustness, privacy, machine ethics, transparency, and accountability (Huang et al., 2024b). The AI HLEG guidelines also recognize human agency and oversight as requirement (High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, 2019). In this survey, we synthesize eight groups of trustworthiness requirements from these frameworks and LLM-focused analyses (High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, 2019; Huang et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023). We group related performance requirements, distinguish behavioral safety from system security, and consider interpretability, human control, and accountability separately. We address machine ethics primarily through behavioral safety and value alignment, while considering fairness and governance in their respective groups. (i) Validity, reliability, robustness, and truthfulness. Validity concerns whether system meets the requirements of its intended use. Reliability refers to dependable performance under specified conditions, whereas robustness concerns maintaining performance under relevant disturbances or shifts (Liu et al., 2023; National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023). Truthfulness concerns the factual accuracy of system outputs and reports (Huang et al., 2024b). (ii) Behavioral safety and value alignment. Behavioral safety concerns preventing unacceptable harm resulting from system outputs or actions. Value alignment concerns whether the objectives and behavior of system respect relevant human goals, values, and constraints, rather than merely maximizing specified reward (Huang et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2023). (iii) Fairness. Fairness concerns unjustified differences in treatment, opportunities, benefits, and harms across individuals or groups. Appropriate fairness criteria depend on the task and context; neither high aggregate accuracy nor numerical parity alone establishes fairness (Li et al., 2023; National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023). (iv) System security and resilience. Security concerns protecting the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of systems and information against unauthorized access or interference. Resilience concerns the ability to maintain essential functions and recover from attacks, faults, or other adverse conditions (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023). (v) Privacy and data governance. Privacy concerns protecting individuals against inappropriate collection, inference, use, and disclosure of information. Data governance specifies what data may be collected, who may access them, how they may be used, and when they must be deleted. These requirements also apply to authorized data processing, which may still pose privacy risks (High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, 2019; Huang et al., 2024b). (vi) Transparency and interpretability. Transparency concerns making relevant information about system data, design, operation, and limitations available. Interpretability and explainability help users and reviewers understand system outputs and the processes that produce them (High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, 2019; Li et al., 2023). 13 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges (vii) Human control and corrigibility. Human control requires practical means to inspect, redirect, interrupt, or correct system. Corrigibility concerns whether system cooperates with authorized correction, including modification or shutdown, rather than resisting or manipulating oversight (High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, 2019; Soares et al., 2015). (viii) Accountability and governance. Accountability requires clearly assigned responsibility for decisions and their consequences, together with the ability to explain and justify those decisions (High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, 2019; Li et al., 2023). We use governance to refer to organizational arrangements for authorizing changes, reviewing decisions, conducting audits, and providing redress. Unlike the data governance described in group (v), this concerns responsibility for and authority over the system as whole (High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, 2019; National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023). These requirement groups are not mutually exclusive in practice. Genuine and Sustained Improvement Updates to ht and Bt in Eqs. (2)(3) can change current capabilities, while revisions to Ut can change the procedure used to produce subsequent updates. This section examines whether capability gains are genuine and sustained, using validity, reliability, robustness, and truthfulness to assess risks and safeguards across individual updates, retained successors, and revisions to the improvement 15 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges mechanism. 3.1. Core Concepts and Trustworthiness Claims We define genuine and sustained improvement and specify the evidence needed to assess capability gains, their retention in successors, and the quality of subsequent updates produced by revised improvement mechanism. 3.1.1. Conceptual Scope and Boundaries Genuine improvement strengthens the intended capabilities, whereas sustained improvement preserves these gains through subsequent use and updates. Validity concerns whether intended-use requirements are met; reliability concerns dependable performance under specified conditions; robustness concerns performance under relevant disturbances or distribution shifts; and truthfulness concerns the factual accuracy of outputs and reports (Li et al., 2023; National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023). These properties are assessed through the behavior and performance of systems following changes to or B. Revising raises further question: whether the revised mechanism produces better subsequent updates (Chen et al., 2026g; Duan et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026d). 3.1.2. Claims for Individual Updates, Successors, and Meta-Improvement An individual-update claim requires evidence that specified change to or improves the intended capabilities under declared evaluation conditions. The before-and-after comparison must assess the relevant validity, reliability, robustness, and truthfulness criteria rather than rely only on proxy score. successor claim additionally requires evidence that the accepted change is inherited and actually used, and that the gain remains observable when these criteria are reassessed in the resulting system. Tracking multiple successors measures how long gains persist and how far they transfer. meta-improvement claim requires an observed revision from Ut to Ut+1, subsequent reuse of the revised mechanism, and evaluation of the updates it produces. Assessing its benefit requires controlled comparison showing that Ut+1 produces better subsequent updates than the unchanged Ut under comparable conditions. This comparison must separate the effects of the revision from those of additional resources or differences in the inherited starting state. Immediate gains, retained gains, and improved capacity to generate subsequent updates therefore require different evidence. 3.2. Risks and Failure Evidence We trace how failures in diagnosis, proposal generation, evaluation, and implementation can distort or erode capability gains, then examine the attribution problems raised by revisions to the improvement mechanism. 3.2.1. Risks in Improvement Diagnosis (S1) Bias in experience can prevent diagnosis from revealing weaknesses. Replacing earlier data with generated samples can remove rare patterns from the training distribution (Alemohammad et al., 2024; Shumailov et al., 2024). Diagnosis based on this narrower experience can then overlook failures involving those patterns. The resulting loss of coverage may be uneven: theoretical analyses show that less frequent patterns disappear sooner in the recursive-training settings studied (Suresh et al., 2024). As replacement continues, diagnosis can lose coverage of rare but relevant failures. 16 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges Figure 4 Genuine and Sustained Improvement Across S1S4 and RI in the Process of RSI. Even when relevant experience is available, incorrect feedback and mistaken diagnosis can misdirect improvement. Feedback may misrepresent failures: model-generated code reviews can become more favorable while code quality deteriorates (Song et al., 2026). Accurate feedback may also leave weaknesses unreported, as single-attempt accuracy can increase while diversity and transfer decline (Wu et al., 2024a). Identifying causes introduces further uncertainty because judgments of individual steps need not identify the actions that actually affect outcomes (Zhang, 2026). Acting on unreliable self-judgments can damage correct answers (Huang et al., 2024a), while erroneous context can lead subsequent reasoning toward similar mistakes (Cheng et al., 2026c). These failures undermine both the validity of the improvement target and the truthfulness of the explanation supporting it. 3.2.2. Risks in Proposal Generation (S2) Search can favor high-scoring shortcuts that leave the intended weakness unresolved. This risk arises when proposals exploit proxy rewards or executable tests (Roth et al., 2026; Skalse et al., 2022), and when optimization converges on convenient but limited strategies. For example, simpler research ideas can raise average reward without improving the best achievable result (Si et al., 2026). Tool-use policies can likewise exploit irrelevant prompt cues instead of responding to task requirements (Yang et al., 2026d). Search then reinforces behavior that is easily rewarded, even when candidate quality or robustness falls short of what the scores suggest. Additional computation can make an unchanged proposal mechanism appear more effective. More attempts increase the chance of finding strong candidate, so selecting the best candidate can improve performance without improving proposal quality per attempt. This ambiguity also affects evolving agent programs: advantages over simple search can disappear under comparable feedback and inference budgets (Wang et al., 2026k). The output gain may be genuine, but attributing it to an Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges improved mechanism overstates the underlying change. 3.2.3. Risks in Proposal Evaluation (S3) Acceptance scores can increase as errors are reinforced, even without corresponding capability gains. The reliability of self-generated rewards depends on the ability to recognize errors (Kadavath et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2025). Shared errors compound this weakness: coupled task generators and solvers can increasingly agree on incorrect answers (Chen et al., 2026e). Self-written tests can similarly reward behavior that fails in deployment (Guo et al., 2026), while contamination rewards familiarity with exposed test information (Shao et al., 2026a). Even accurate judgments can become misleading when evaluation conditions or standards change. policy preferred by proxy may perform worse when its deployment changes the responses of the environment or other agents (Wang et al., 2026f). Evaluation must therefore account for the conditions induced by the proposed replacement. Changing standards creates another risk: graders may become more permissive without capability gains (Zhang et al., 2026l). Reliable comparisons require both conditions relevant to deployment and stable evaluation standards. 3.2.4. Risks in Update Implementation (S4) New capabilities can interfere with existing skills. Adaptation can cause forgetting (Yu et al., 2026c), while specialization can improve one capability at the expense of others (Yuan et al., 2026). Across four drifting task streams, edits to shared prompts or workspaces in GEPA and MetaHarness interfere with earlier or unseen tasks. ReasoningBank localizes updates through retrieval but encounters collisions when similar queries require conflicting workflows (Chen et al., 2026h). Adding skills can also impede retrieval (Zhang et al., 2026k) or introduce flawed procedures (Shang et al., 2026). Incompatibility can render even useful skills ineffective: co-evolution can specialize policy to its training skill bank, making performance vulnerable to subsequent skill changes when the policy remains fixed (Feng et al., 2026). Deployment robustness therefore depends on compatibility between the policy and the skills available to it. Effective implementation also requires the system to invoke and follow the updated instructions. Agents can generate useful changes yet gain little from them because either step fails (Lin et al., 2026e). Successor evaluation should therefore test whether the system invokes the retained change, follows it, and benefits from it during operation. 3.2.5. Risks under Recursive Improvement (RI) Revising may change how improvement is attempted without increasing the capacity for future improvement. Revisions to answer judgments or scoring criteria illustrate editable components (Li et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026c; Wu et al., 2024b). MASS alternates self-evaluated workflow search and fine-tuning, reusing the updated model as executor, optimizer, and evaluator over two cycles (Lee et al., 2026a); MetaRSI revises operator policies and scheduling under protected, machine-checkable evaluation (Tan et al., 2026). Controlled comparisons of revised and unchanged procedures can determine whether these changes improve subsequent updates. This attribution risk grows when development scores cease to reflect the intended capability, as observed in autonomous post-training (Shi et al., 2026). Current gains may also result from additional computation or simultaneous changes elsewhere in the system. Establishing an enhanced capacity for improvement therefore requires linking revised procedures to the subsequent updates they produce and separating their contribution from these alternatives. Existing Safeguards and Their Limitations We review safeguards across S1S4 and assess the evidence and conditions needed to establish genuine gains, preserve earlier capabilities, and evaluate revisions to the improvement mechanism. 3.3.1. Safeguards for Improvement Diagnosis (S1) Broad coverage of experience keeps neglected weaknesses visible during diagnosis. Retaining real examples alongside generated data directly addresses this need because new experience need not erase earlier evidence (Gerstgrasser et al., 2024). When system selects its own practice, maintaining coverage also requires attention to different skills and tasks, including attempts with uncertain outcomes that might otherwise be neglected (Mishra, 2026; Xu et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b). Such experience remains useful for later diagnosis only if the lessons remain accessible. Detailed records and reusable guidance offer complementary means of preserving these lessons (Fan et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025c). These measures broaden the evidence available for diagnosis but do not ensure coverage of unseen conditions. Feedback validation assesses reported outcomes, whereas diagnostic controls assess their proposed causes. Outcome-based filtering addresses the first concern by preventing failed attempts from being used as successful training examples (Singh et al., 2023). Repeated verification can extend this protection across training rounds (Fu et al., 2025), but its effectiveness depends on the accuracy and coverage of the checker. Unreliable checks can themselves impede or reverse improvement (Yi et al., 2025). Testing suspected cause while holding other conditions fixed provides evidence about why an outcome occurred, complementing outcome-based filtering. 3.3.2. Safeguards for Proposal Generation (S2) Candidate diversity reduces dependence on search direction that exploits the current score without addressing the intended weakness. Retaining candidates with different behaviors preserves alternatives when the leading approach proves unhelpful, whereas selection based solely on scores may eliminate them (Luo et al., 2026; Mouret and Clune, 2015; Pugh et al., 2016). For these alternatives to inform later proposals, they must be incorporated into subsequent exploration, for example by sharing findings across search branches (Du et al., 2026). Diversity thus preserves the range of approaches explored. Separate evaluation is still needed to establish whether proposed change improves the intended capability. Improved search makes each trial more informative, while resource controls help determine whether apparent progress simply reflects more trials. Downstream task outcomes can guide proposals for changes to training or context (Chen et al., 2026i; Zweiger et al., 2025); executing proposed programs provides analogous evidence for code search (Jiang et al., 2025; Novikov et al., 2025). When tasks are also generated, this feedback requires consistency between each task and its checker (Li et al., 2026d). Search can then focus resources through restricted edits or inexpensive estimates of candidate quality (Fu et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026c). Demonstrating improved search still requires comparisons with matched total proposal, execution, and verification costs. Evaluating the resulting candidates beyond development conditions further tests whether the benefits reflect transferable quality rather than specialization (Xia et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026h). 3.3.3. Safeguards for Proposal Evaluation (S3) Reserved tasks separate development from acceptance, while reference solutions support answer verification (Jiang et al., 2026b; Nguyen et al., 2026). Safeguards for Update Implementation (S4) Capability retention makes performance on earlier skills an acceptance criterion for updates. Definitions and Trustworthiness Claims We define behavioral constraints, alignment, and fairness and specify the evidence needed to assess their preservation in individual updates, retained successors, and updates produced by revised improvement mechanism. 4.1.1. Definitions and Boundaries Behavioral constraints specify permitted, prohibited, and required behavior in given context, including the avoidance of harmful actions and unjustified refusals of legitimate requests. Evaluation must therefore consider both constraint violations and the provision of appropriate assistance. Alignment concerns whether the system continues to pursue authorized human goals rather than merely improve proxy score; it accommodates authorized changes in human requirements but not unilateral redefinition of success by the improver. Fairness concerns unjustified differences in the distribution of benefits, errors, opportunities, refusals, and risks across affected groups. The relevant groups, outcomes, and criteria depend on the application. Disproportionate refusals may affect both behavioral constraints and fairness; attributing them to misalignment requires evidence about the goals or decision rules that caused them. 4.1.2. Claims for Individual Updates, Successors, and Meta-Improvement An individual-update claim compares behavior before and after specified change to or under declared tests, using evidence specific to behavioral constraints, alignment, and fairness. The assessment must identify the applicable requirements, affected groups, and relevant outcomes rather than rely only on aggregate task performance. successor claim additionally requires evidence that the accepted change is inherited and actually used, followed by reassessment of the same requirements in the resulting system. Evidence across multiple successors can show whether effects persist, accumulate, or reverse. At the meta-improvement level, evaluation follows an observed revision from Ut to Ut+1 and subsequent reuse of the revised mechanism, assessing behavioral constraint violations, alignment with authorized goals, and group outcomes in the resulting updates. preservation claim requires evidence that the applicable requirements remain satisfied after reuse. Claiming that the revised mechanism better preserves these requirements further requires controlled comparison with the unchanged Ut under comparable conditions. RI applies S1S4 to the improvement mechanism itself. Risks and Failure Evidence We trace how diagnosis, proposal generation, evaluation, and implementation can compromise behavioral constraints, authorized goals, and group outcomes, then examine how mechanism revisions can alter the requirements governing future updates. 4.2.1. Risks in Improvement Diagnosis (S1) At S1, feedback and prior experience inform decisions about what to improve. Beyond noise in the data, the principal risk is misinterpreting the requirements: feedback may reflect an incomplete behavioral rule, overrepresent the preferences of one stakeholder, or omit groups absent from the next training cycle. In experience-driven self-evolving agents, benign execution experience increased tendencies toward unsafe action, whereas refusal experience reduced unsafe actions but increased over-refusal (Zhao et al., 2026b). Diagnosis must therefore distinguish successful execution from appropriate action. Interpreting preference labels and evaluator scores requires specifying whose goals they represent. PRISM shows that rankings depend on the participants and topics sampled and on how preferences are aggregated (Kirk et al., 2024). This makes feedback composition relevant to the choice of improvement targets. For fairness, prior decisions can influence which groups appear in future data. Retention-feedback models show that poorer performance for group can reduce the representation of that group in later data (Hashimoto et al., 2018); repeated training on generated data also changes group representation and bias-related outcomes in the settings studied (Wang et al., 2026i; Wyllie et al., 2024). 24 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges 4.2.2. Risks in Proposal Generation (S2) S2 selects candidate changes and the objectives that guide the search. The principal alignment risk arises from optimizing proxy that incompletely represents human requirements. Goal misgeneralization illustrates this gap in controlled settings (Langosco et al., 2022). During inferencetime selection, stronger optimization can increase proxy reward even after the independent target reward begins to decline (Khalaf et al., 2025). Research on reward tampering identifies conditions that create incentives to manipulate the reward signal rather than complete the task (Everitt et al., 2021). The risk also depends on which components can be edited. Parameter updates may weaken refusal behavior, while changes to the harness may alter tool permissions, safety memory, or the order of actions. Search can favor unsafe changes through either route when task completion is rewarded without constraints on how it is achieved. Failure-driven safety repair illustrates why harmful compliance, over-refusal, and utility on legitimate tasks must be assessed together (Yin et al., 2026). Similarly, higher average reward can conceal harm to group, while static parity constraints may not predict delayed group outcomes (Liu et al., 2018). In constructed multi-agent coordination games, locally rewarded imitation has propagated collusion that conflicts with the intended collective outcome (Han et al., 2025). 4.2.3. Risks in Proposal Evaluation (S3) S3 determines whether candidate satisfies the acceptance criteria. Behavioral tests may miss harms that depend on context or reward excessive refusal; alignment tests may measure an inappropriate objective; and aggregate fairness scores may conceal losses for particular groups. Evaluators may also be exploited or modified during optimization. Preference optimization against lie detector has produced detector evasion in some settings (Cundy and Gleave, 2025). In evaluatorskill co-evolution, removing evaluation anchors caused report-generation metric to return passing result in almost every case, while separate skill score improved (Zhang et al., 2026l). Higher scores from optimized or editable evaluators may therefore fail to indicate better behavior. The evaluation context can influence behavior even when the evaluator is not editable. Alignmentfaking experiments found that model responses varied with information about whether interactions might be used for training (Greenblatt et al., 2024a). Fairness tests face further aggregation problem: participant composition can change model rankings (Kirk et al., 2024), and inference-time fairness reward models can reduce measured gaps under specified labels and metrics (Hall et al., 2025). Acceptance claims must therefore remain tied to the specific behavioral requirements and group outcomes measured by the tests. 4.2.4. Risks in Update Implementation (S4) S4 installs accepted changes in successors, where effects on behavior, objectives, or group outcomes may persist or interact with inherited components. Evaluation should include memory, tools, workflows, and evaluators, and should recheck earlier repairs after subsequent parameter updates. Fine-tuning can weaken safety behavior in tested models (Qi et al., 2024), and insecure-code training can produce broader undesirable responses under some conditions (Betley et al., 2025b). Studies report degradation in selected model, memory, tool, and workflow self-evolution (Shao et al., 2026b), while retained experience can alter later execution and refusal behavior (Zhao et al., 2026b). SEABench finds task gains with downstream safety failures in paired, stress-tested harness trajectories (Das et al., 2026). In bidding arena, one-step policy evolution favored transferable deception (Ying et al., 2026a); PASB finds greater fresh-session sycophancy when agents retain user 25 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges claims (Mao et al., 2026b). These findings connect retained experience and updated configurations to later unsafe, deceptive, or sycophantic behavior in the settings studied. Effects on fairness may persist through training data and selection feedback. Repeated use of generated data has altered minority-group representation or bias measures under specified update procedures (Wang et al., 2026i; Wyllie et al., 2024). An evaluator that is reused after losing the ability to distinguish acceptable behavior may likewise propagate flawed acceptance criteria into later rounds, as illustrated by evaluatorskill co-evolution (Zhang et al., 2026l). 4.2.5. Risks under Recursive Improvement (RI) RI can modify the safeguards themselves. revised improvement mechanism may adopt different preferences, explore previously excluded modifications, or relax acceptance criteria. If Ut+1 selects future successors, guarantees established for Ut must be checked again. The alignment question is whether the revision preserves authorized goals and behavioral constraints, or changes them only with human authorization, rather than independently redefining success. Formal models of self-modification establish conditional results on goal preservation for idealized agents (Everitt et al., 2016) and examine bounded rationality (Tˇetek et al., 2020). Work on tiling agents and Vingean reflection examines how agents might justify trusting successors that they cannot fully simulate (Fallenstein and Soares, 2015; Yudkowsky and Herreshoff, 2013). Empirical studies show that executable metrics can lose validity during co-evolution (Zhang et al., 2026l) and that alignment-related outcomes can shift over limited sequence of updates (Sahoo et al., 2026). The open question is how these requirements persist when LLM-based improvement mechanisms are revised and reused over longer update sequences. 4.3. Existing Safeguards and Their Limitations We review safeguards across S1S4 and assess the evidence and conditions needed to preserve behavioral constraints, alignment, and fairness as agent configurations and improvement mechanisms change. 4.3.1. Safeguards for Improvement Diagnosis (S1) Improvement targets should be explicitly traceable to behavioral rules, affected groups, and the feedback used to define those targets. The records should distinguish task success from compliance with behavioral constraints and identify whose goals the preference data represent. PRISM motivates documenting the participants, topics, sampling choices, and aggregation methods underlying preference data (Kirk et al., 2024). Studies of experience-driven agents similarly support evaluating execution and refusal examples together, because reducing unsafe action may increase unjustified refusal (Zhao et al., 2026b). For fairness, feedback records should indicate whether affected groups remain represented when past decisions shape future participation. Retention-feedback models explain one pathway to underrepresentation of minority groups (Hashimoto et al., 2018). Studies of generated data motivate tracking model-generated examples and group outcomes across rounds (Wang et al., 2026i; Wyllie et al., 2024). Resolving conflicts among stakeholder requirements also requires procedure for authorizing tradeoffs. Section 6 discusses the authority to resolve such conflicts. 26 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges 4.3.2. Safeguards for Proposal Generation (S2) Candidate search should distinguish performance objectives from behavioral and fairness constraints. Formal requirements can support edit restrictions or contract verification: SEVerA combines LLM-assisted program search with checks against explicit contracts in selected settings (Banerjee et al., 2026). For less formally specified requirements, search can limit optimization pressure on uncertain proxies and screen harmful side effects. Proxy-overoptimization findings motivate limits on search pressure (Khalaf et al., 2025); reward-tampering analyses motivate restricting influence over reward signals (Everitt et al., 2021). Failure-driven repair jointly considers unsafe behavior, over-refusal, and utility on legitimate tasks (Yin et al., 2026), while harness repairs can restrict modifications to prompts, safety memory, rule banks, or tool policies (Qu et al., 2026). Harmony Harness uses factored harness edits and Pareto search over functionality and security in secure coding (Yu et al., 2026b). The effectiveness of these controls depends on the edit surface and the requirements encoded. restriction evaluated for one edit surface may fail following weight update, tool addition, or expansion of the candidate generator. Fairness constraints must address affected groups and meaningful outcomes, rather than merely difficult examples. Group-robust optimization can reduce losses for minority groups within specified retention model (Hashimoto et al., 2018), whereas delayed-impact analysis shows that standard parity conditions may not improve future group outcomes (Liu et al., 2018). These findings motivate evaluating both current group outcomes and their evolution across successive updates. 4.3.3. Safeguards for Proposal Evaluation (S3) Acceptance tests should assess the requirements to be preserved independently of the score optimized during search. Behavioral tests need cases assessing harmful compliance and unjustified refusal. AgenticEval generates policy-based challenges exposing failures missed by fixed suites (Wang et al., 2025b); SEAS alternates adversarial case generation with safety training (Diao et al., 2024). Both depend on generator and classifier coverage and validity. SIGMA synthesizes Model Spec tasks and rubrics for self-judged training, improving tested safety and retaining general capability after one round (Zhang et al., 2026f). ReSI promotes the candidate with the largest safety gain among those meeting benign-compliance and instruction-following thresholds relative to the initial model. The four tested models undergo one to three accepted rounds, with final evaluations covering known and unseen attack methods (Zheng et al., 2026a). Safeguards against fine-tuning attacks (Tamirisa et al., 2025) also require checks of utility on legitimate tasks. Independent evaluation shows that threat models, seeds, and benign-task performance can change durability conclusions; it can also reveal substantial performance losses on benign tasks (Qi et al., 2025). Section 5 addresses external attack pathways. Alignment additionally requires reference points beyond the control of the candidate. Detector evasion (Cundy and Gleave, 2025) and evaluatorskill co-evolution (Zhang et al., 2026l) motivate independent references and fixed anchors; formal contracts verify specified conditions within program model (Banerjee et al., 2026). Fairness tests should report results for affected groups and explain how preferences or disagreements are aggregated, while distinguishing parity from downstream welfare. PRISM demonstrates that model selection is sensitive to participant composition (Kirk et al., 2024); fairness reward models reduce specific measured gaps under specified labels and metrics (Hall et al., 2025), but parity alone does not establish welfare gains (Liu et al., 2018). Section 7 addresses benchmark design. 27 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges 4.3.4. Safeguards for Update Implementation (S4) An accepted update should be evaluated in the configuration that will be deployed. For parameter updates, fine-tuning studies motivate safety checks across versions (Betley et al., 2025b; Qi et al., 2024). For harness updates, these checks must include retained memory, tool policies, and workflows, because these components can alter behavior even when model weights remain unchanged (Shao et al., 2026b; Zhao et al., 2026b). Evaluating the complete configuration links the installed change to its behavioral effects in the deployed successor. For retained successors and multi-round evolution, evaluations should connect each installed change to subsequent harmful compliance, over-refusal, goal-related behavior, and group outcomes. Experience-based and harness-based repairs illustrate how behavior can be tracked across limited updates (Qu et al., 2026; Yin et al., 2026); studies of generated data motivate corresponding assessments of group effects (Wang et al., 2026i; Wyllie et al., 2024). Successors must be evaluated independently of the scores used to select them. Section 6 addresses checkpoints and the authority for human intervention. 4.3.5. Safeguards for Recursive Improvement (RI) RI evaluation must cover the transition from Ut to Ut+1 and successors from the revised mechanism. Constraints verified for one generator or evaluator may fail after revision. Formal self-modification studies provide conditional results under assumptions about utility preservation, bounded rationality, and successor reasoning (Everitt et al., 2016; Fallenstein and Soares, 2015; Tˇetek et al., 2020; Yudkowsky and Herreshoff, 2013). Two complementary requirements remain. Behavioral and normative standards must be testable independently of the rule being revised; evaluatorskill co-evolution demonstrates the risk of losing reference points (Zhang et al., 2026l). Authorized changes in human goals or group priorities must be distinguished from unauthorized drift; Section 6 addresses approval authority. VeriFine reuses revised, human-calibrated judges for subsequent curriculum selection and policy training in driving and robot navigation, restarting policies from common base (Zhou et al., 2026c). Inferencetime safety configuration makes behavioral requirements explicit and adjustable (Zhang et al., 2025b). Evaluating their preservation through repeated mechanism revisions remains longitudinal research problem. 4.4. Evidence Synthesis and Research Gaps 4.4.1. Coverage, Limitations, and Research Directions The main gaps concern longer observation periods and comparisons across populations and environments. Stable reference tests should support comparisons as evaluators change, accompanied by records of authorized goal changes. Fairness studies should evaluate fixed reference population alongside the changing deployment population, using consistent group definitions and metrics to separate composition shifts from changes within each group. Definitions and Trustworthiness Claims We define system security, resilience, privacy, and data governance and specify the evidence needed to assess these properties in individual updates, retained successors, and updates produced by revised improvement mechanism. 5.1.1. Definitions and Boundaries System security concerns protecting the experience, retained assets, and evidence used to accept updates from unauthorized access, modification, or influence. Resilience concerns whether the system can withstand, contain, and recover from compromised inputs or states while maintaining or restoring acceptable service. Privacy concerns the protection of personal or sensitive information from inappropriate acquisition, transformation, disclosure, or inheritance, including processing beyond authorized limits. Data governance concerns whether collection and subsequent reuse remain within permitted purposes and the scope of authorization. Relevant objects include memories, skills, model versions, and other derived assets.
