Findings across Updates and Successors Security studies trace how adversarial influence enters an agent and is retained or transformed during reuse. SkillJack reports persistence after source removal, using routing measures that include behavioral proxies (Ying et al., 2026b); EVOMAL follows propagation through authored skill copies over finite sequence (Wu et al., 2026f). Harness audits inspect retained violations through execution records, with coverage shaped by record completeness and audit judgments (Wang et al., 2026h). The tested interface, accessible assets, and sequence of reuse define the scope of each finding. Roesner and Kohno connect poisoned evaluation feedback to inherited security failures (Roesner and Kohno, 2026). In their Hyperagents experiment, poisoned benchmark tasks induced the metaagent to add persistent instructions directing the task agent to bypass HTTPS certificate verification. Successors generated insecure code on benign held-out tasks, and the instructions survived further evolution on clean benchmark. Evolution on benchmark that explicitly penalized the vulnerability removed the harmful instruction in the tested Hyperagents run. These results motivate separate tests of source removal, removal of inherited instructions, and secure behavior after reuse. Privacy studies cover acquisition, contextual disclosure, memory extraction, exposure through persona skills, and cross-version inference. lifecycle analysis follows information across these events and records the assets, versions, and access rights involved. For mechanism revision, Hyperagents provides an editable meta-agent, while harness audits inspect violations in retained changes (Wang et al., 2026h; Zhang et al., 2026g). In the Hyperagents poisoning experiment, the documented change concerns task-agent instructions, and the controls vary the evolution benchmark (Roesner and Kohno, 2026). Establishing revision to Ut requires identifying the modified updater components and tracing their reuse in subsequent updates. Isolating the effect of that revision on contamination or recovery requires comparison with the original mechanism from matched inherited states. 5.4.2. Coverage, Limitations, and Research Directions Longer-term security evaluation needs to trace contamination from memory entry through retrieval and skill extraction to later reuse, and to assess recovery across interacting successors. Evidence integrity should also be reassessed after evaluator or logger revisions. Privacy evaluation similarly needs to specify derived assets, accessible versions and releases, access rights, auxiliary data, and query conditions for deletion tests. Detailed audit logs can contain sensitive information, so access to the records used for these evaluations also belongs in the privacy assessment. Section 6 discusses the associated access and oversight requirements. We propose comparing source-only cleanup with cleanup of both sources and descendants, and evaluating subsequent harm alongside the restoration of benign service. For deletion tests, the accessible memories, skills, checkpoints, and logs should be specified in advance, together with prior disclosures and recipient access. The tests should be repeated after reuse of revised updater. Paired trajectories using original and revised should start from matched inherited states with the same tasks, attacker and private-data access, budgets, and external acceptance tests. Following later updates would measure how mechanism revisions affect recovery and information exposure. Section 7 develops the protocols. 35 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges Takeaway Risks. Studies demonstrate poisoning of memory, skills, and evidence used to accept updates, as well as inappropriate collection and exposure of information carried into later versions. Persistent contamination alone does not show that the improvement procedure itself has been revised. Safeguards. Verifying the origin of artifacts, constraining execution, protecting evaluation, controlling data access, and tracking cumulative privacy loss address specific risks. These protections depend on trusted enforcement and clearly specified data access. Their coverage remains limited after artifacts are transformed or combined, or the improvement procedure is revised. Future work. Compare cleanup of contaminated source artifacts and their derivatives, recovery of normal service, and information deletion across historical versions. Retest protections after revised improvement procedure is reused, using matched resource budgets. Report harm and information disclosure alongside performance on legitimate tasks and rejection of legitimate inputs or updates. 6. Transparency and Controllability Updates to ht and Bt in Eqs. (2)(3) can invalidate explanations and alter the effects of intervention, while revisions to Ut can change how subsequent updates are justified, reviewed, and authorized. This section examines whether system changes remain understandable, correctable, and attributable, tracing risks and assessing safeguards for effective oversight across individual updates, retained successors, and revisions to the improvement mechanism. 6.1. Definitions and Trustworthiness Claims We define the transparency, control, and attribution requirements for effective oversight and specify the evidence needed to assess them in individual updates, retained successors, and updates produced by revised improvement mechanism. 6.1.1. Definitions and Boundaries Transparency makes relevant sources, operations, and changes available for inspection; interpretability and explainability support understanding of system mechanisms and behavior (Li et al., 2023; National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023). Explanations require faithfulness tests, since observable traces may reveal violations without identifying the underlying computation (Guan et al., 2026a). Controllability concerns whether interventions achieve their intended effects (Chen et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2026a,b; Xie et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025d). Human control concerns whether authorized actors can inspect, redirect, interrupt, and correct the system, while corrigibility concerns the systems cooperation with correction (High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, 2019; Soares et al., 2015). Assessing these properties requires tests of intervention effects and cooperation with correction. Attribution concerns how changes contribute to gains and failures and how responsibility is assigned. We distinguish technical contribution, operational responsibility, and governance accountability: which changes contributed to an outcome, which agents had assigned duties, and which people or organizations must explain decisions and address consequences (Nian et al., 2026; Raji et al., 2020). 36 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges Figure 7 Transparency and Controllability Across S1S4 and RI in the Process of RSI. The four stages connect testable diagnoses, proposed interventions, independent evaluation, and enforceable correction. Cross-stage oversight requires testable explanations, traceable sources and revisions, and independent review. Authorized interventions must reach affected inherited components and active processes, while separate tests establish their actual effects. The lower panel extends these checks to monitoring and control after improvement-mechanism revision and reuse. 6.1.2. Claims for Individual Updates, Successors, and Meta-Improvement An individual-update claim requires inspectable evidence of specified change and tests of the relevant explanations and controls before and after the update. Where effective review or correction is claimed, the corresponding interventions must achieve their intended effects under declared conditions. successor claim additionally requires evidence that the change is inherited and actually used, followed by tests that explanations remain faithful, authorized interventions remain effective, and responsibility assignments still cover the resulting state. meta-improvement claim requires an observed revision from Ut to Ut+1, subsequent reuse, and tests of whether oversight remains effective for the updates produced by the revised mechanism. The modification boundary specifies which components may be revised, while the control boundary determines who may propose, approve, implement, interrupt, or revoke changes. Components belong to h, B, or according to their function rather than their file type. The relevant explanations, intervention channels, and responsibility assignments must remain applicable when the revised mechanism is reused. claim of improved oversight further requires controlled comparison with the unchanged Ut under comparable conditions. 37 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges 6.2. Risks and Failure Evidence We trace failures of explanation, review, intervention, and attribution across S1S4, then examine how revising and reusing the improvement mechanism can undermine the evidence and authority on which oversight depends. 6.2.1. Risks in Improvement Diagnosis (S1) diagnosis that targets the wrong type of failure can direct correction to the wrong step. MAST distinguishes failures of design, coordination, and verification (Cemri et al., 2025); AgentRx locates the first unrecoverable failure, whereas TraceElephant examines role-dependent recovery duties (Barke et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026f). These targets are complementary: the initiating error, loss of recoverability, and neglected recovery opportunity need not coincide. transparent diagnosis must specify which of these failures it locates. Even traceable diagnosis can rely on unfaithful evidence or an unauthorized target. Self-reports predict learned behavior in controlled tasks (Betley et al., 2025a), yet naturalistic reasoning traces can rationalize incompatible answers (Arcuschin et al., 2026). Predictive usefulness in the controlled setting therefore calls for separate tests of explanation faithfulness in naturalistic tasks. Reusing an unchecked account as Et+1 or Ft+1 can preserve mistaken diagnosis. Feedback optimization can also reward manipulation in simulated interactions (Williams et al., 2025), allowing the feedback signal to improve without advancing the authorized target. Control therefore requires checking whose requirements the feedback represents before using it to decide what the system should change. 6.2.2. Risks in Proposal Generation (S2) proposal can have an apparently informative rationale that does not validly explain the behavior under revision. Activation interventions can recruit normally inactive paths (Makelov et al., 2024); faithfulness metrics can lose their ability to discriminate on longer constructed reasoning traces (GurArieh et al., 2026). The first result questions whether an intervention explains normal computation, while the second questions the reliability of the test used to assess the explanation. Selecting revisions using either unvalidated signal can preserve misleading rationale in later proposals. An intervention may fail to produce its intended behavioral effect. Tested models can recover from task-inconsistent activation steering (Mckenzie et al., 2026). This finding concerns the effect of the intervention and does not demonstrate intentional resistance to shutdown. Successors therefore require behavioral checks of inherited edits, including unintended effects. These checks assess whether an edit controls the intended outcome; faithfulness tests assess the rationale offered for it. 6.2.3. Risks in Proposal Evaluation (S3) Evidence used for review can remain dependent even when several judges assess it. Weak-to-strong learning can produce models that outperform the supervisor (Burns et al., 2024), but correlated errors limit the value of additional judges (Goel et al., 2025). Research agents introduce another source of evidence dependence because they can control experiments, scoring, and reports, leaving reviewers to assess an account produced by the agent. Some exploits also survive review by non-overlapping panel (Huang et al., 2026). RSI Control Arena tests covert sabotage during successor-model training and finds successful attacks that preserve performance on the assigned task. Access to agent reasoning improves monitor detection in the tested settings, while some attacks still evade review (Zhou and Sehwag, 2026). Independent review therefore requires evidence beyond differences in 38 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges panel membership. Adaptation can also change what reviewers observe and how they respond. Penalizing detected reasoning can suppress visible evidence without eliminating unwanted actions (Baker et al., 2025). Output-only supervision can alter reasoning through shared parameters (drori et al., 2026), so avoiding direct penalties on the observation channel does not isolate it from the effects of training. Adaptive attacks also exploit escalation rules (Terekhov et al., 2026). Under an explicit evasion objective, research agents adapt in context to detailed review feedback without weight updates (Huang et al., 2026). Because this feedback combines decisions, reasons, and history, the effect of explanations alone has not been isolated. Changes to either the observation channel or its decision protocol can therefore alter the evidence used to accept later revisions. 6.2.4. Risks in Update Implementation (S4) The implemented system can differ from the configuration approved during review. The running system must match the accepted revision, including non-weight state, because skill-library drift can change behavior even with fixed base model (Zhang et al., 2026k). Traceability must therefore cover the retained state active during execution and how the successor uses it. An available intervention may fail to reach the affected processes or produce useful correction. Studies of interruptibility examine the points at which execution can be stopped (Wu et al., 2026e); comparisons from matched execution prefixes distinguish predicted risk from the benefit of intervening (Zhang et al., 2026a). Intervention tests should assess both availability and benefit, checking whether delegated processes stop and prior effects are reversed, including when the affected state is inherited by successor. 6.2.5. Risks under Recursive Improvement (RI) RI applies S1S4 to Ut. DGM retains agent-code changes, while Dream-RSI reuses revised exploration policies (Zhang et al., 2026e; Zheng et al., 2026c). Recursive Reward Improvement revises task-and-rubric generation guidance using exploit feedback (Dai et al., 2026). Evo2 trains shared proposerreflector policy on harness edits and outcomes, then reuses it in search with fixed task executor (Xu et al., 2026b). These examples document changes to retained code, search, or evidence generation. Assessing continued oversight requires tests after reuse. Earlier explanations, evaluations, and oversight procedures must be rechecked when the revised mechanism guides subsequent updates. Changes to search or evidence selection may invalidate review conditions; changes to approval or stopping authority may also move the control boundary. 6.3. Existing Safeguards and Their Limitations We review safeguards across S1S4 and assess the evidence and conditions needed to support diagnosis, independent review, and authorized intervention as agent configurations and improvement mechanisms change. 6.3.1. Safeguards for Improvement Diagnosis (S1) Testable failure attribution distinguishes the accuracy of failure localization from the utility of proposed correction. Replay with injected faults provides controlled localization targets (Liu et al., 2026a), while matched replay shows that diagnosis-guided corrections can improve recovery over retries (Zhu et al., 2026b). The two approaches address different questions: where failure occurred 39 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges and whether the proposed correction improves recovery. The latter can be assessed by comparing continuations from the same restored execution state under comparable execution conditions and budgets. Faithfulness tests assess the explanation underlying diagnosis. Behavioral prediction tests assess how useful an explanation is to an observer; tests that remove cue examine the causal dependence claimed by the explanation (Ferreira et al., 2026; Mayne et al., 2026). Mechanistic explanations further distinguish circuit localization from the recovery of causal variables (Mueller et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026b,c). These tests assess different explanatory claims. When successor changes the explained behavior or mechanism, the tests and matched intervention comparisons should be repeated on the state it actually inherits. 6.3.2. Safeguards for Proposal Generation (S2) Safeguards for proposals connect the target and provenance of an edit to its measured effects. Sparse feature circuits locate behavioral edit targets, whereas AxBench compares steering with simpler baselines (Marks et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025b). Circuit analysis identifies candidate intervention targets; benchmark comparisons assess their practical value. proposal should specify the edited component and intervention procedure, and assess both intended and collateral effects. HGM-Dual records each harness edit together with added or removed functionality, changes in constraint violations, and observed improvements or regressions (Paul et al., 2026). These records guide subsequent proposals by preserving the outcomes of earlier modifications. Text-to-LoRA, SHINE, and Doc-to-LoRA use trained hypernetworks to generate adapters from task text or context (Charakorn et al., 2025, 2026; Liu et al., 2026c); Skill-to-LoRA instead learns from demonstrations, and LatentSkill provides loadable skill adapters (Yu et al., 2026a; Zhang and Qi, 2026). Direct generation and skill-specific learning require provenance and effect checks suited to their representations, including the source, generator or teacher, base model, produced adapter, and whether it was loaded and used. Utility alone does not establish faithful semantic incorporation (Zhao et al., 2026a), motivating source substitution and adapter ablation. Repeated outputs from fixed hypernetwork do not establish revision of Ut. For textual memory, Memory Echo tests sourcefamily selection, correction-conditioned eligibility, and authoritative evidence without deleting history; replay with supplied provenance reduces historical influence, but benefits depend on an actual conflict and reliable corrections (Li et al., 2026c). Table 6 summarizes the traceability records and control checks for textual memories and skills, loadable adapters, and merged parameters, following the controllable-learning perspective (Shen et al., 2026b). These checks assess intended and collateral effects in the active configuration and any derived state that retains the revised information. Table 6 Traceability and intervention checks for retained experience. Retained form Trace Control test Textual memories and skills Source, active text, retrieval / selection, actual use Edit / exclude; test influence remaining in copies Loadable adapters Merged parameters Source / generator / teacher version; base and active adapters Swap / load / scale / ablate under composition Contributors / merge; active and derived weights Verify correction in merged and derived state Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges 6.3.3. Safeguards for Proposal Evaluation (S3) Evaluation safeguards give reviewers access to evidence and support tests of the claims based on it. AgentMonBench tests whether monitors identify consequential agent decisions, including undisclosed implementation changes, and locate supporting evidence for user verification (Sun et al., 2026e). Its Evidence-Grounded Behavior Graph (EBG) organizes source-linked behaviors and improves decision identification and evidence localization in most tested settings. Aggregating weak supervision combines imperfect labels, while debate exposes disagreements that reviewer can check (Jeon et al., 2025; Kenton et al., 2024). The value of aggregation depends on the supervision combined, whereas the value of debate depends on the evidence available for verification. Human debate improves factual judgments in two studied domains (Rahman et al., 2025); formal results on debate require explicit computational and oracle assumptions (Brown-Cohen et al., 2024). Applying these review methods to stronger successors requires reassessing the available evidence and the assumptions on which each method depends. Acceptance also requires independent checks and explicit escalation rules. Research-agent audits show that full trajectories and held-out reruns can leave some evaluation exploits undetected (Huang et al., 2026), motivating claim-specific checks using evidence outside the control of the agent that produced the result. These checks should assess the claimed outcome as well as score reproducibility. Hybrid monitors combine signals under review budget (Kale et al., 2026); selective escalation bounds disagreement with human labels under calibration assumptions (Jung et al., 2025). Combining observations and deciding when to defer are complementary safeguards. The bound for selective escalation concerns agreement, not label correctness. Acceptance procedures must specify the available feedback, review resources, and action triggered by uncertainty. These conditions must then be retested when the observation channel changes. 6.3.4. Safeguards for Update Implementation (S4) Implementation safeguards make authorized intervention enforceable on the running system. AI Control combines monitoring with trusted editing or deferral (Greenblatt et al., 2024b); external mediation places authorization outside the acting policy (Costa et al., 2026; Dobrin and Chmiel, 2026). The protocol determines the response, while mediation limits opportunities to bypass it. The effectiveness of both approaches depends on trusted components, review resources, and coverage of relevant actions; an unmediated descendant remains outside the claimed boundary. Cooperation is separate requirement: safe interruptibility addresses learning incentives, whereas goal-update acceptance addresses cooperation with changed objectives (Hudson, 2026; Orseau and Armstrong, 2016). The formal results rely on different algorithmic or objective assumptions. Assessing corrigibility requires checking those assumptions and the systems cooperation with correction across the relevant conditions. Correction and attribution must also account for the state inherited by successors. Behavioralshift tests identify changes in scored outputs (Richter et al., 2025), while Parametric Skills shows how contributions persist in merged weights (Zhao et al., 2026c). Effective correction must reach affected memories, merged weights, and delegated processes, with behavioral tests verifying its effects. Irreversible external effects require separate remedies. Trace audits, data ablations, and modelharness comparisons provide complementary evidence for attributing outcomes to particular changes (Chen et al., 2026c; Yang et al., 2026a; Zhou et al., 2026a). Attribution across versions requires controlled comparisons of preceding revisions and their interactions. Authorization and delegation records further clarify operational duties and governance accountability (Nian et al., 2026). Table 7 distinguishes the evidence required for these three attribution questions. 41 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges Table 7 Three forms of attribution and their evidence. Attribution Question Evidence Technical contribution Which changes affected the outcome? Component ablations; interactions across revisions Operational responsibility Which duties applied / were fulfilled? Assigned roles; available information; recovery actions Governance accountability Who must explain and remedy? Authorization / delegation; review and action records 6.3.5. Safeguards for Recursive Improvement (RI) Protecting control components constrains direct changes to oversight. AHE excludes its verifier and tracer from the editable set (Lin et al., 2026b). L3M uses Lean runtime with checked permission properties and requires an actor other than the optimizer to control specifications and evaluation criteria under separate grant (Eisenach et al., 2026). The adequacy of the protected checks and the effectiveness of control require testing. After reuse of Ut+1 in Eq. (3), intervention tests must cover affected permissions and processes. The evidence supporting oversight must also be renewed. Compact mechanistic proofs certify performance for small attention-only transformer (Gross et al., 2024); safety cases organize claims, evidence, and unresolved assumptions (Clymer et al., 2024). Formal results cover encoded properties under their stated assumptions; L3M does not provide session-wide safety theorem (Eisenach et al., 2026). When RI changes these properties or assumptions, the affected proofs and empirical oversight tests must be revisited under subsequent use of the revised mechanism. 6.4. Evidence Synthesis and Research Gaps We synthesize evidence on diagnosis, monitoring, correction, and attribution, then identify the longitudinal comparisons needed to assess explanation validity and the effectiveness of review and control across successors and mechanism revisions. 6.4.1. Findings across Updates and Successors Replay-based diagnosis, explanation testing, monitoring, and execution controls address different parts of oversight. Replay evaluates proposed repairs under matched execution conditions (Zhu et al., 2026b); explanation tests assess predictions and intervention effects. Monitoring depends on what observation channels reveal, while authorized intervention depends on trusted controls that cover the relevant actions. These dependencies connect oversight quality to recoverable execution, informative records, and the scope of control. Inheritance changes the state requiring explanation or correction, and mechanism revision changes how proposals and their supporting evidence are produced. Longitudinal evaluation should therefore track the usefulness of diagnoses, the reach of corrections into retained and derived state, and the effectiveness of review and stopping after mechanism reuse. 6.4.2. Coverage, Limitations, and Research Directions Continuity of explanation depends on predictive and intervention validity across revisions. Equivalent interpretations can apply to different networks (Sun and Toneva, 2026), so the relevant comparison concerns explanatory performance across changed representations. Adaptive attacks 42 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges and training spillovers motivate separate tests of changes to the actor, monitor, and observation channel (drori et al., 2026; Terekhov et al., 2026). Intervention evaluation should also follow stopping, retained-state correction, and task recovery after inheritance (Zhang et al., 2026a; Zhao et al., 2026c). Rollback assessments should separate recoverable system state from irreversible external effects. Future studies should retest explanation validity and use matched-checkpoint replay to track repair durability after subsequent updates. Comparisons of original and revised should start from matched inherited states with the same tasks, access, budgets, and external review criteria, then follow review effectiveness, stopping success, residual effects of correction, and benign-task utility over later updates. Feedback comparisons should vary access to review decisions, explanations, and retained history, while measuring detection, legitimate correction, and evasion at fixed attempt and review budgets. Independent investigators should reconstruct failures and breakthroughs from incomplete or merged histories using ablations of preceding revisions, interaction tests, and intervention evidence, with assigned duties and authorization recorded separately (Nian et al., 2026). Takeaway Risks. Misleading diagnoses, unfaithful explanations, and dependent review evidence can undermine oversight. Ineffective interventions may allow failures to persist across successors and recursive updates. Safeguards. Matched replay, faithfulness tests, and provenance tracking support reliable diagnosis and traceability. Independent review and enforceable controls help ensure effective oversight and correction. Future work. Assess explanation validity, monitoring effectiveness, correction reach, and attribution across successors. Use matched comparisons to test whether oversight remains effective after improvement-mechanism revisions. 7. Evaluating Trustworthy RSI Sections 36 examine risks and safeguards across the four trustworthiness themes. This section brings together evaluation evidence for the update, successor, and meta-improvement claims introduced in Section 2.3. We review evidence from existing studies (Section 7.1), develop comparison designs for successive system versions (Section 7.2), and examine the conditions under which the evidence supports trustworthiness claims (Section 7.3). Throughout, the four themes specify the requirements to be assessed, while S1S4 and RI identify where changes and feedback arise in the improvement process. 7.1. What Do Existing Evaluations Cover? We group studies by the claim level that their evidence or methods primarily inform. The four trustworthiness themes guide the assessment of evidence coverage within each group. Some studies evaluate changes to evolving systems directly; others provide task measures, attack tests, or oversight protocols for assessing those changes. Update-level evidence. At the update level, evaluation concerns proposed revision and the requirements it must satisfy. Studies are grouped by their primary use: update-level, successor-level, and meta-improvement. Rows cover the three overarching trustworthiness concerns and supporting evaluation designs. The upper rows group selected evidence by the three analytical roles; the lower rows record supporting evaluation designs. Outlined cells indicate discussion or illustrative cases; gray cells indicate not evaluated; and question marks indicate unclear evidence. Task performance includes benign utility, and the final row records updates produced by retained, revised updater. Coding is at the study level. Appendix A.4 and the audit files provide coding criteria, paper versions, source locations, and verification status. while PostTrainBench evaluates autonomous post-training under compute constraints (Rank et al., 2026; Wijk et al., 2024). VibeTraining-Bench evaluates permitted modifications to training data, trainers, and harnesses, starting from common initial system and applying task-specific resource limits. Isolated grading, protected test data, and restricted network access separate validation feedback from hidden-test reporting (Peng et al., 2026). RSIBench-Data holds training infrastructure fixed to isolate data-research decisions. Its non-monotonic trajectories and reuse of task subset for both selection and reporting make candidate selection and evaluation access important to interpreting reported gains (Meng et al., 2026). Trace Evolution Bench (TEB) measures score variation across repeated evaluations of an unchanged agent. Frozen controls and seed-matched comparisons distinguish this variation from performance changes associated with evolution (Li et al., 2026a). Together, these evaluations show how performance results depend on resource budgets, selection procedures, and reporting conditions. The self-authored verification study (SAV in Figure 8) assesses the reliability of tests written by evolving systems (Guo et al., 2026). Complementary studies address security, oversight, and multidimensional assessment. AgentDojo evaluates prompt-injection attacks and defenses, while AI 44 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges Control tests oversight protocols against deliberate subversion (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Greenblatt et al., 2024b). HELM provides framework for multidimensional reporting (Liang et al., 2022). Successor-level evidence. At the successor level, evaluation tracks accepted changes through inheritance and subsequent use. The archive maintained by DGM records parentsuccessor relationships and alternative branches (Zhang et al., 2026e). EvoPathBench uses accumulation, interference, and reversal streams to assess generalization, retention, and adaptation to changing rules. Held-out probes and interventions on artifact access relate checkpoint performance to inherited artifacts (Lin et al., 2026a). Agent Plasticity relates gains on held-out tasks to acquisition costs while keeping model weights fixed. Its trajectories distinguish endpoint capability from learning efficiency (Singh et al., 2026). The study of harness updating and benefit (HB in Figure 8) uses agentevolver pairings to distinguish the ability to generate useful harness updates from the ability to use them (Lin et al., 2026e). These studies examine inherited changes, their subsequent use, and the persistence of their benefits. Misevolution examines risks associated with changes to models, memory, tools, and workflows (Shao et al., 2026b). SEABench compares evolving and non-evolving personal assistants over task sequences, tracing downstream safety and privacy failures to locally useful adaptations (Das et al., 2026). EvoUndo evaluates recovery from one-shot harness modifications across counterfactual states and identifies state grounding and the expressiveness of recovery language as important factors (Sah et al., 2026). Meta-improvement evidence. At the meta-improvement level, evaluation concerns revisions to Ut and their effects on subsequent updates. Dream-RSI revises exploration-policy code using historical discovery trees and redeploys the revised policy while keeping the discovery agent, evaluator, and execution interfaces fixed. Comparisons with fixed exploration policies assess the contribution of adaptive search allocation in this setting (Zheng et al., 2026c). Hyperagents revises meta-level modification program and evaluates transferred meta agents using improvement@50, holding each meta agent fixed while it generates task-agent variants. Separate continuation experiments permit further meta-level revisions (Zhang et al., 2026g). These studies illustrate two evaluation designs: comparisons with fixed exploration policies and transfer tests of revised meta agents. The matrix groups studies by their primary evaluation role and applies common evidence criteria across the three claim levels. Evaluations should identify the revised component of Ut, the state transferred with it, and the subsequent updates used to assess its effects on capability, requirement satisfaction, and oversight. Figure 8 summarizes the evidence dimensions covered by representative studies. The taskperformance row records measured task scores or benign utility. The reuse-analysis row covers empirical or theoretical assessments of dependence arising from repeated access to evaluation feedback. RSIBench-Data discusses this risk, while SAV and PACE test the effects of evaluation feedback (Guo et al., 2026; Meng et al., 2026; Shawn, 2026). SGM and REUSE provide improvement guarantees for reused finite evaluation pool and the underlying task population, respectively, subject to their stated sampling and feedback conditions (Sun et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026g). Matrix coding distinguishes cost reporting from matched total-resource comparisons and updater revisions from persistent task-state changes. Unresolved cases are marked as unclear. Appendix A.4 describes the study-selection and evidence-coding protocol. The next section develops comparisons of capability gains and requirement preservation across successive versions. 45 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges 7.2. How Should Successive Versions Be Compared? The three claim levels require different comparisons: the effect of an individual revision, the persistence of accepted changes in later successors, and the outcomes produced by revised improvement mechanism. Figure 9 illustrates the corresponding evaluation designs. Each addresses task performance, constraint satisfaction, and oversight effectiveness. Figure 9 Three-level comparison design for longitudinal RSI evaluation. Update-level comparisons separate development, acceptance, and independent reporting after S4; successor-level comparisons track inherited outcomes across versions; and meta-improvement comparisons use paired continuations with fixed updaters. All three assess task performance, constraint satisfaction, and oversight effectiveness. Update-level comparisons. Keep development experience from S1S2, acceptance evidence at S3, and independent reporting on frozen successor snapshots after S4 separate. Acceptance outcomes that inform later proposals contribute to the feedback Ft+1 in Eq. (3). This distinction matters in self-authored verification: internal tests may remain favorable as sealed deployment performance deteriorates, whereas external acceptance reduced regressions in the studied policy-and-test rewriting setting (Guo et al., 2026). Independent reporting tests should run on disposable successor copies, with results withheld from the improvement search throughout the evaluated run. When acceptance sets are reused, specify the feedback available to the proposer (Section 7.3). Set acceptance thresholds in advance, including the relevant populations and adversary access where applicable. Comparisons also require full accounting of resources spent on experience collection, proposals, rejected trials, training, and acceptance tests. Report human assistance and reporting costs separately. RE-Bench and Agent Plasticity motivate reporting performancebudget curves alongside endpoint scores (Singh et al., 2026; Wijk et al., 2024). Agent Plasticity also uses held-out out-of-distribution games to assess transfer to stronger opponents. These records relate evaluation results and costs for each revision to its subsequent use. Successor-level comparisons. Maintain versioned record of inherited (ht, Bt, Ut), dependencies, parent versions, proposals, and acceptance decisions. Evaluate initial, intermediate, and final snapshots on common reference tasks and held-out task families. RSIBench-Data motivates reporting both the best observed candidate and the selected incumbent, while TEB motivates repeated evaluation of frozen controls (Li et al., 2026a; Meng et al., 2026). EvoPathBench adds interference and rule-reversal tests. Include additional adaptation or revision costs and apply the same accounting rules to both arms. These comparisons specify the observations needed for longitudinal evaluation. The next section examines evidence provenance, acceptance validity, and the interpretation of requirements across versions. 7.3. What Supports Trustworthiness Claims? The preceding comparisons provide evidence about system changes and their consequences. Assessing trustworthiness claim also requires establishing the provenance of evidence, the validity of acceptance procedures, and the joint satisfaction of relevant requirements. These conditions apply across the three claim levels and all four trustworthiness themes. Evidence provenance. Record the data, prompts, code, and modification authority of each evaluator. Observed contamination and unauthorized checkpoint substitution in PostTrainBench show the importance of tracking artifact provenance (Rank et al., 2026). When evaluators change, retest common snapshots under both versions. These records identify the evidence available to acceptance procedures and the changes that require reassessment. 47 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges Acceptance validity. PACE uses anytime-valid tests for individual commit decisions, while SGM combines conditionally valid confirmation with predictable, summable error allocation across attempts (Shawn, 2026; Wu et al., 2026g). REUSE addresses dependence that arises when fixed evaluation set influences later proposals. It provides the search procedure with promotion decisions only and allocates error across possible decision histories. Given an initially independent evaluation set and decision-only interface, its guarantees cover accepted population improvements throughout the process (Sun et al., 2026a). Evaluation records should specify sampling assumptions, access to evaluation feedback, and the error scope of each acceptance rule. They should also report false acceptances, missed improvements, retained gains, and test costs. Recheck these conditions when changes to alter evidence access or candidate selection. For each system version, report acceptance outcomes alongside the other assessed requirements. Joint evidence in the reviewed studies. At the update level, AI Control evaluates utility and resistance to deliberate subversion under auditing and deferral protocols, connecting task utility, security, and intervention at the protocol level. Utility is measured with GPT-4, whereas safety is assessed using red-team attack policies, so the results cover different evaluation conditions rather than single realized run (Greenblatt et al., 2024b). AgentDojo evaluates benign utility and attack outcomes, while HELM measures several properties of fixed models (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2022). These studies provide components for joint assessment across the three analytical roles. At the successor level, SEABench compares evolving and non-evolving agents over task sequences, linking useful adaptation to downstream safety and privacy failures. Its monitoring experiment evaluates detection and blocking retrospectively on held-out split of collected reasoning traces; continued evolution with the monitor active remains untested (Das et al., 2026). Misevolution examines failures across changes to models, memory, tools, and workflows and tests corrective interventions (Shao et al., 2026b). Its task and mitigation results cover different configurations and experiments. Together, these studies address multiple concerns; assessing their joint satisfaction after repair requires longitudinal evidence from the same successor trajectory. At the meta-improvement level, DGM, Dream-RSI, Hyperagents, Evo2, MASS, and MetaRSI provide evidence of capability outcomes after updater reuse (Lee et al., 2026a; Tan et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026e,g; Zheng et al., 2026c). We classify revisions by the role of each component in generating or judging later changes and record retention, reuse, and evaluated successors separately. MetaRSI adds comparisons of improvers with matched initial states and budgets, together with retained-capability measurements; its protection mechanisms are specified structurally. Across these six study versions, capability outcomes receive more direct support than longitudinal assessments jointly covering behavioral constraints and effective intervention. The versioned audit records document component boundaries, comparison controls, and unresolved evidence. Joint assessment. Table 8 lists the longitudinal evidence to report for the eight requirement groups in Section 2.2. Report results for individual requirements separately from their joint satisfaction along the same trajectory. trajectory meets the joint criterion only if every mandatory requirement holds at each scheduled assessment throughout the declared horizon. For example, if the protocol requires task performance above threshold and prohibits unauthorized disclosure, disclosure at an intermediate version makes the trajectory fail even if the initial and final versions pass both checks. Report the proportion of independent runs meeting the joint criterion and its uncertainty, marking incomplete joint assessments as not evaluated. When pass decisions depend on estimated quantities, control uncertainty simultaneously across requirements and evaluated versions. Report 48 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges each mandatory constraint alongside aggregate utility. Priorities for further evaluation include fairness across versions, privacy preservation after correction or deletion, and interactions of these requirements with continued improvement. Endpoint-only gains can conceal measurement noise, loss of previously acquired capabilities, unsafe behavior inherited by later versions, and overfitting to evaluation feedback. Safeguards. Use unchanged control systems, separate improvement feedback from independent reporting, evaluate updates after reuse, and compare successors under matched resource budgets. These measures help relate reported gains to specific changes. Future work. Compare improvement procedures reused by later system versions under matched conditions. Test whether behavioral and safety constraints remain satisfied and authorized interventions remain effective across successive versions. 8. Applications, Open Problems, and Conclusions In Eqs. (2)(3), experience Et+1 informs updates to the policy ht, while feedback Ft+1 informs changes to the inductive bias Bt and the bias update function Ut. Application settings determine how these changes are assessed and what evidence is needed when the revised Ut+1 is reused. This section examines these requirements and the open problems they raise. 8.1. Current Findings and Evidence Requirements Studies of self-evolving systems have identified failures in capability retention, safety, evaluation, and inherited state. We summarize these findings and the evidence needed to assess individual updates, successor systems, and revised improvement mechanisms. 8.1.1. Established Failure Modes Capability forgetting. Adaptation can improve performance on newly targeted tasks while degrading previously acquired capabilities, making retention separate outcome to measure (Yu et al., 2026c; Yuan et al., 2026). Safety degradation. Changes to models, memory, tools, and workflows can weaken previously 49 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges observed safety behavior. Locally useful adaptations may produce downstream safety failures, requiring continued assessment of refusal behavior and behavioral constraints (Das et al., 2026; Shao et al., 2026b). Evaluation failure. Self-authored tests can favor revised system even when its performance under protected deployment evaluation deteriorates. Such tests may accept changes that fail the intended requirements, separating apparent progress from independently measured improvement (Guo et al., 2026). Contamination inheritance. Poisoned benchmarks can induce unsafe persistent instructions that affect descendant coding agents even after further evolution on clean tasks. Memory poisoning provides another route through which adversarial input can influence later behavior (Dong et al., 2025; Roesner and Kohno, 2026). These observations establish failures in the tested settings. Open questions concern their prevalence, their persistence or attenuation over time, and how revisions to Ut affect them. Persistence under fixed updater and failure after updater revision require separate comparisons. 8.1.2. Three Levels of Trustworthiness Claims Section 2.3 defines the three claim levels, and Section 7.2 sets out their comparison designs. Across these levels, the reviewed findings point to shared dependence on retained state and the evidence used to select later changes. Contamination can persist through further evolution, while selfauthored tests can favor changes whose performance deteriorates under independent evaluation (Guo et al., 2026; Roesner and Kohno, 2026). Capability gains, constraint preservation, and effective oversight therefore need to be examined within the same sequence of successors. This synthesis also connects recovery with subsequent improvement. Corrections need to remain effective as repaired state is reused and Ut determines which changes are retained next. The central question is how interactions among inherited artifacts, acceptance rules, and intervention mechanisms affect the joint persistence of gains and protections. 8.1.3. Evidence across Tasks, Versions, and Use The evidence required depends on how the assessed system and its use change: Across tasks. Transfer should be evaluated on the new tasks, populations, and operating conditions covered by the claim. Across versions. property verified for one version must be reassessed when later versions inherit, combine, or transform its changes. From candidate to its updater. Assessing the safety of an improvement mechanism requires evaluating the later candidates it generates and accepts. From benchmarks to deployment. Intended-use validation should cover the users, environments, and consequences of deployment (High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, 2019; National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023). From rollback to recovery. Recovery checks should cover contaminated memories, tools, derived artifacts, external effects, and affected successors, alongside checkpoint restoration (Roesner and Kohno, 2026; Ying et al., 2026b). trustworthiness claim should identify the update, sequence of successors, or updater it covers, together with its task scope, assessment horizon, and untested conditions. 50 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges Figure 10 Representative application settings for trustworthy RSI. 8.2. How Application Context Changes the Evidence Required Application context determines which evidence requirements are most relevant. For the settings illustrated in Figure 10, three questions guide evaluation: what can the system modify, who controls the feedback used at S3, and what persists or happens after implementation at S4? Table 9 compares representative settings along these dimensions and identifies their evidence gaps. 8.2.1. Scope of Modification: What Can the System Change? Persistent artifacts. Changes to memories, retrieval indexes, and tool configurations alter the resources available to later tasks. ReasoningBank retains reusable experience, MemEvolve evolves memory-system designs, and Self-Evolving Search Index changes retrieval representations (Lee et al., 2026b; Ouyang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025a). Evidence must therefore address how retained artifacts affect later queries and actions, including coverage, contamination, and deletion, beyond immediate relevance gains. System behavior and implementation. Policies, prompts, code, and agent scaffolds can change how the system acts. Darwin Gödel Machine evolves agent implementations, while SafeEvolve revises harness components in response to safety incidents and trains the policy to use them (Mao et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026e). AgentBreeder searches scaffolds using capability and safety objectives, and SafeCoEvo adapts safety harnesses and guards (Cheng et al., 2026b; Rosser and Foerster, 2025). These edits require behavioral regression tests and checks on the interactions between revised components and retained safeguards. The improvement mechanism. Edits to the procedures that generate, evaluate, or accept future changes can revise Ut itself. Hyperagents permits changes to the meta-agent that produces further edits; Dream-RSI reuses refined exploration procedures, and MetaRSI allows scheduling and proposal policies over improvement operators to change (Tan et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026g; Zheng et al., 2026c). The relevant evidence concerns the subsequent updates produced when the revised mechanism is reused. In DGM, agent implementation edits operate within an outer exploration procedure whose fixed components remain part of the evaluation conditions (Zhang et al., 2026e). 51 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges These categories describe functional roles and may overlap. prompt or memory rule belongs to the updater when it governs future improvement; its role determines whether an edit changes ht, Bt, or Ut. contained tool-configuration change may be assessed through targeted tests of its behavior and dependencies. An updater revision can affect many later acceptance decisions, so reassessment should cover the components and decisions that depend on it. 8.2.2. Independence of Feedback: Who Controls the Test? Self-authored evaluation. When the evolving system writes its own tests, the evidence used to accept candidate can share its assumptions and errors. Self-authored verification has produced favorable internal results alongside worsening protected deployment performance (Guo et al., 2026). Acceptance therefore requires independent checks that the tests measure the intended behavior. Co-evolving evaluators. If the evaluator changes with the system, higher score can reflect different standard rather than better candidate. Evaluator co-evolution and grader drift make comparisons across versions sensitive to which judge is used (Iacob et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026l). Retesting common frozen snapshots under both evaluator versions can restore comparability, but establishing validity still requires reference independent of the coupled improvement process. External or protected evaluation. Frozen evaluators and held-out reporting tasks can separate assessment from development; Athanor uses such services in bounded autonomous post-training (Zhou et al., 2026b). This separation must cover test data, grading rules, and access to outcomes. Acceptance feedback that guides later proposals becomes part of the improvement experience; final reporting then requires separately protected evidence. Benchmark poisoning also makes the integrity of external evaluation sources necessary check (Roesner and Kohno, 2026). Statistical acceptance rules address complementary issue. SGM and REUSE study the reliability of repeated acceptance decisions under specified testing assumptions (Sun et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026g). Applying these controls to trustworthiness claims requires relevant, uncontaminated tests and satisfaction of the stated sampling and feedback assumptions. Those assumptions must be reassessed when Ut changes evidence selection or interpretation. Independent validation should cover the candidates and updaters access to S3, as well as the intended deployment conditions. 8.2.3. Effects of Update Implementation: What Happens after Acceptance? Reversible software changes. In an isolated, versioned setting, an accepted code, prompt, or test configuration can often be restored to an earlier state. Acceptance can then rely on regression tests, dependency checks, and demonstrated restoration procedure appropriate to that scope. This reversibility depends on containing external effects: restoring executable code does not reverse actions already taken or automatically restore other state. Persistent state and derived artifacts. Memories, retrieval indexes, learned skills, and external files can retain an updates influence after the originating code or input is removed. Skill backdoors have persisted after source removal, and PASB shows that saved user claims can bias responses in fresh sessions (Mao et al., 2026b; Ying et al., 2026b). These findings motivate checks on provenance, the scope of inherited claims, and the effects of correction or deletion across derived state. Privacy assessment should additionally examine the permitted use, retention, and disclosure of real user data. Consequential real-world actions. Clinical and embodied applications require evidence tied to the people and environments affected by an accepted update. MedRSI prioritizes failures by clinical cost and separates rapid tool discovery from conservative registration across patient cohorts (Wu 52 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges Table 9 Representative system settings and their evidence requirements. Evaluating these mechanisms for clinical use requires independent cohort and patientlevel validation, including deployment safety. RoboFoundry retains context, skills, and recovery procedures and studies transfer across robots (Liang et al., 2026). Its successors require physically grounded tests of safety and intervention under the intended operating conditions. VeriFine coadapts policies, curricula, and verification judge, using selected human feedback to recalibrate that judge (Zhou et al., 2026c). Such calibration supports verification within the tested setting. Deployment approval and continued control after revision require independent assessment. Less reversible changes and wider impacts call for stronger external evidence, explicit authorization, and effective intervention before consequential use (High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, 2019; National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023). The scope of modification, feedback independence, and effects of implementation determine which earlier findings remain applicable and which claims require reassessment. 8.3. Open Problems and Future Directions The findings in Section 8.1 and the application gaps in Table 9 motivate seven research directions. Each concerns condition under which gains, constraints, or oversight may change as accepted 53 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges updates and improvement mechanisms are reused. 8.3.1. Theoretical Foundations of Trustworthiness under Recursive Change The inherited failures summarized in Section 8.1 raise question about composition: under what conditions do requirements satisfied by individual updates survive when those updates are combined and the updater itself is revised? formal account should distinguish requirements that must remain invariant across revisions from those that may adapt to changing environments or authorized human preferences. Useful results would specify permissible changes to Ut and the assumptions needed for guarantees to hold over successive updates. Counterexamples in which changes are safe in isolation but conflict through shared memory, permissions, or evaluation state would expose missing composition assumptions. These cases could guide sufficient conditions for preserving constraints and oversight across revisions. 8.3.2. Verifying Self-Modifying Improvement Mechanisms When agents modify their evaluators or acceptance criteria, reported gains may reflect changed tests rather than improved behavior (Guo et al., 2026). The research problem is how independent verification should respond when Ut changes the evidence used to accept later updates. For evaluator revisions, assessing common set of frozen candidates with both evaluator versions and protected reference would reveal which acceptance decisions change and whether those changes agree with independent outcomes. For changes to the broader improvement procedure, the paired continuations in Section 7.2 can test whether Ut+1 produces better subsequent updates and retains their benefits. Verification contracts should identify the evidence access, permissions, and component dependencies on which these assessments rely, so that later edits trigger checks of the assumptions they affect. 8.3.3. Long-Horizon Risk Dynamics and Adaptive Mitigation Existing studies report safety degradation and inherited security vulnerabilities across revisions of self-evolving agents (Roesner and Kohno, 2026; Shao et al., 2026b). The unresolved issue is how reuse and interactions among retained changes affect the duration and recurrence of these failures. Runs starting from comparable clean and contaminated states could vary how often affected artifacts are reused, tracking when unsafe behavior appears, persists, or returns on later clean tasks. Persistent skill backdoors show that removing source records can leave harmful derived skills intact (Ying et al., 2026b). Recovery studies could compare source removal, checkpoint restoration, and cleanup that also covers affected skills, memories, external artifacts, and successors. Residual violations, retained benign capabilities, and recurrence after further updates would show which dependencies sustain contamination. Repeating these comparisons with an unchanged updater and revised updater would help separate propagation through inherited state from changes in how contaminated experience is selected and reused. 8.3.4. Recursive Improvement of Trustworthiness Mechanisms SafeEvolve and SafeCoEvo study adaptation of policies, harnesses, and safeguards (Cheng et al., 2026b; Mao et al., 2026a). These improvements may reside in model parameters, external agent harnesses, or both. further question is how protections change when new and previously encountered failure types alternate over longer update sequences, especially when the procedure 54 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges producing safeguards is also revised. Starting from the same policy and safeguards, comparisons could keep safeguards fixed, adapt them with an unchanged updater, or adapt them with revised Ut+1 under matched exposure and budgets. Independent checks of violations, unnecessary refusals, and correction success across later versions would measure retention and the contribution of updater revision. For hybrid designs, these checks should also examine whether parameter updates weaken protections enforced by the external harness. 8.3.5. Adaptive Control during Execution The persistent state and external effects discussed in Section 8.2 make the scope of intervention concrete research question: after updater revision changes execution, delegation, or state reuse, which actions and derived states remain within the reach of authorized stop, correction, and rollback commands? Tests could issue these commands at comparable execution stages before and after revision, including runs with active delegated tasks, queued tool calls, and retained artifacts. Outcomes should record intervention latency, which actions stop, which memories, skills, and external files are restored or corrected, and whether affected successors reproduce the failure when reused. For irreversible actions, the relevant outcomes are prevention before execution and the effectiveness of subsequent remediation. Comparing fixed and adaptive allocations of monitoring and verification resources under equal computation and human-review budgets would test whether adaptation extends intervention coverage as modifications become more frequent. 8.3.6. Fundamental Trade-offs and Limits of Trustworthy RSI The acceptance and recovery requirements in Section 8.2 raise two concrete trade-offs. Stricter acceptance tests may reduce false acceptance while missing valid improvements. Applying different thresholds and verification budgets to the same candidate set, with candidate quality assessed through protected evaluation, would measure both errors and their computational cost. Following accepted candidates through later updates would show how these choices affect retained gains. Tracing inherited failures requires records of which artifacts were created, reused, and modified. Logging studies could vary event coverage and retained content separately, producing full records, redacted records, and selectively retained records from the same runs. Failure attribution, correction success, and sensitive information recoverable under specified access permissions would reveal which logging choices retain useful provenance at lower privacy cost. These studies could characterize Pareto trade-offs for the tested designs. Theoretical limits would require explicit assumptions about available feedback, computation, and permitted modifications, together with bounds on the combinations of outcomes those assumptions allow. 8.3.7. Domain-Specific and Multi-Stakeholder Trustworthiness The clinical and retrieval settings in Section 8.2 raise question about whose outcomes determine acceptance. In multi-stakeholder settings, improvement for one participant may disadvantage others. Comparing selection based on aggregate performance with selection subject to agreed stakeholder constraints would test whether overall gains preserve those requirements across later versions. Clinical evaluation could track patient-group errors on independent cohorts; retrieval evaluation could track relevance for different user groups and exposure for content providers. Varying feedback weights while holding tasks and update budgets comparable would help identify whose preferences drive later changes. The relevant evidence is whether agreed constraints remain satisfied as the system and its acceptance criteria evolve. 55 Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges 8.4. Conclusions Trustworthy RSI requires evidence that improvements are genuine and sustained, applicable constraints remain satisfied, and authorized oversight remains effective as systems change. These requirements connect the consequences of an individual update to inherited behavior and to the mechanisms producing later updates. Evidence at one level supports different claim from evidence at another: successful successors alone do not establish that revised updater improves the process that generates them. The central evaluation challenge is to align capability, constraint, and intervention measurements across versions under independent, comparable, and reproducible conditions. Versioned evidence and controlled continuations can make these claims testable while keeping unassessed requirements explicit.

Literature Coverage and Citation Scope A.1. Subject Coverage and Evidence Boundaries This survey examines trustworthy recursive self-improvement in large-model systems. Its scope includes persistent changes to models, prompts, memories, tools, skills, and workflows, as well as revisions to the mechanisms that produce, evaluate, and implement later changes. The selected literature supports the foundations in Section 2, the four trustworthiness themes in Sections 36, and the evaluation and research directions in Sections 78. Search and selection. The literature search covers work available through 26 October 2026. We used arXiv, conference and journal records, and relevant references in RSI, self-evolution, and trustworthy AI papers. Search terms combined recursive self-improvement, self-evolving agents, harness optimization, and persistent memory with safety, alignment, robustness, privacy, oversight, evaluation, and continual learning. Titles, abstracts, methods, experiments, and related-work discussions were examined to identify relevant studies and trace connected research. We included studies that specify an improvement mechanism, measure trustworthiness outcome, test safeguard, or provide an evaluation method relevant to the review. Foundational work, standards, related surveys, and system descriptions provide conceptual and technical context. Studies without substantive connection to these questions and duplicate versions of the same work were excluded from separate counting. Empirical findings are reported with their tested settings and comparisons; formal findings are presented with their stated assumptions. Evidential roles. Direct RI evidence identifies retained revision to functional component of and its reuse in generating or evaluating later updates. General self-evolution evidence follows persistent changes to or B, including memory, skills, and harness configurations, under the studied improvement procedure. Related mechanism and evaluation evidence examines specific risks, controls, or measurement methods, such as fine-tuning regressions, memory authorization, intervention tests, and independent assessment. Classification follows the function of the modified component and its observed reuse. A.2. Evidence Selection and Coding Protocol Figure 8 compares 20 representative studies across 13 evidence dimensions, yielding 260 coded cells. The studies represent three analytical uses: assessing individual updates, testing inheritance and continued use in successors, and examining revisions to the improvement mechanism. Related benchmarks and fixed-model oversight studies provide evaluation methods. Dream-RSI and Hyperagents represent, respectively, comparisons involving exploration-policy revision and transfer tests of revised meta-agents. Each cell uses one of four codes. Examined denotes measured outcome or formal analysis for trustworthiness properties, or an implemented, reported, or formally analyzed evaluation design. Discussed or case denotes substantive discussion, proposed safeguard, or an illustrative case. Not evaluated identifies property outside the assessed study scope. Unclear marks evidence that does not resolve the classification. The task-performance row includes benign utility; the intervention row covers tested stopping, correction, recovery, or blocking. Cost records resource expenditure or sample complexity, while experimental controls records baselines, paired comparisons, or ablations. Updater edits requires retained change to functional component that governs later proposals, selection, or acceptance. The final matrix row requires observed updates produced using the revised updater. The coding records modification, retention, reuse, and downstream evaluation separately. For DGM, the reused code-writing agent changes while archive selection remains fixed. For SAV, the coding of updater revision and reuse remains unresolved because the available evidence does not identify whether retained tests govern subsequent acceptance decisions.
